title: Ch-K-M

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-Tz-R: yatzar, to form, like a potter, and yetzer, the impulse. Your line was form. Did one urge get a turn on the wheel before you acted? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

The person in your family who can fix anything. The aunt who knows exactly what to say at a funeral. The grandfather who rarely gives advice, but when he does, it lands. None of them may have a degree in anything. English would call them handy, or tactful, or sharp. Hebrew can use one word for all three: chochmah. Wisdom. And the Torah uses it, in a striking way, for a craftsman. Today's root: chet, kaf, mem. Ch-K-M. Wisdom with its sleeves rolled up.
screen: `THE ONE WHO CAN FIX ANYTHING.` → `THE ONE WHO KNOWS WHAT TO SAY.` → `CH-K-M: WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Turn this root four ways. First, the hands. When the tabernacle is to be built in the wilderness, God says of the craftsman Bezalel, "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." Wisdom, there, is chochmah, and it lives in the hands: cutting stones, carving wood, working gold. A few chapters later, the women who spin for the tabernacle are called wise-hearted. Wisdom, in the Torah, can be a skill. Second, the beginning. The book of Proverbs, one of the Bible's books of wisdom, sets a starting line: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Some readers hear fear there as closer to awe: knowing you are not the center of everything. In this reading, cleverness without awe isn't wisdom yet. Third, the learner. In Pirkei Avot, the same Ben Zoma who asked who is honored asks another short question: who is wise? He answers, the one who learns from every person. Not the one with the most answers. The one with the most teachers. Fourth, the asking. Proverbs puts it this way: the fool is sure his own way is right, while the wise one listens to advice. So wisdom isn't only something you have. It's something you go and get, from someone else. Put the four together and chochmah looks less like a trophy on a shelf and more like a craft. Practiced with your hands, rooted in awe, learned from anyone, and asked for out loud.
screen: `THE HANDS: BEZALEL'S CRAFT.` · `THE BEGINNING: AWE FIRST.` · `THE LEARNER: FROM EVERY PERSON.` · `THE ASKING: THE WISE ONE LISTENS.` · then, large: `חָכְמָה`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask a wise person's advice. Settle, and breathe. Think of a question you've been carrying alone. A decision, a worry, a conversation you don't know how to start. Then think of someone whose judgment you trust. Not the smartest person you know, necessarily. The one with chochmah in their hands, or in how they listen. Shape the question in a sentence or two, simply, the way you'd actually say it to them. If you pray, you can ask for an understanding heart before you ask them. The bell holds the time.
Ch-K-M. Chet, kaf, mem: the root of chochmah, wisdom, and chacham, a wise person. In the Torah, it can be the skill of a craftsman's hands. Today's word.
Your line: wisdom. Today, send your question to the person you chose, and learn one thing from someone you didn't expect to learn from. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: In Jewish life a learned scholar is called a talmid chacham, a student of the wise, and Jews often study Pirkei Avot, including Ben Zoma's teaching on who is wise, on Shabbat afternoons in the summer.
